paragraphs.text: TO MY MOST DEVOTED LORD AND BROTHER, LUCIDUS THE PRIEST, WHOM I VENERATE AND ESTEEM WITH SPECIAL AFFECTION, FAUSTUS.

It is a great act of charity to prefer to cure the error of a brother who has not been careful enough, by God's grace and help, rather than to cut him off from unity, as the chief bishops are contemplating. What can I say to your Unanimity about this view by letter, as you wish, when I was never able to draw you to the way of truth in person, through long, gentle and humble conversation? So when we speak of God's grace and human obedience, we must above all settle this: that we neither lean to the left nor press stubbornly to the right, but rather walk the royal road. I was surprised, however, that your Reverence said that no one who had taken religious vows had ever written or preached against the catholic faith. In fact a great many people who nonetheless boasted of the Christian name have even thought fit to set down their many profane errors in writing. I will therefore say briefly, as far as I can when speaking to someone absent, what you ought to hold with the catholic church. You should always join the work of the baptized servant to the Lord's grace, and you should detest, along with the doctrine of Pelagius, anyone who asserts predestination in a way that excludes human effort.

Anathema, then, to anyone who, among Pelagius's other impieties, contends with damnable presumption that man is born without sin and can be saved by effort alone, and to anyone who believes that he can be set free without God's grace.

Likewise anathema to anyone who asserts that a man has perished in Adam and through original sin if he was solemnly baptized with a faithful confession and professes the catholic faith, but has afterwards fallen through the various pleasures and temptations of this world.
Likewise anathema to anyone who says that man is driven down into death by God's foreknowledge.
Likewise anathema to anyone who says that the one who perished did not receive the means of being saved [that is, a baptized person, or a pagan old enough to have been able and willing to believe].
Likewise anathema to anyone who says that a vessel made for dishonor cannot rise up to become a vessel for honor.
Likewise anathema to anyone who says that Christ did not die for all and does not will all people to be saved.

But when you come to us in Christ's name, or when you are summoned by the holy bishops, then, if the Lord so commands, we will bring forward suitable testimonies, each in its proper place. They will make plain what is catholic and destroy what is contrary to the catholic faith. Through Christ's illumination, however, we assert truly and confidently two things. First, the one who perished through his own fault could have been saved through grace, if he had not refused that grace the obedience of a servant's labor. Second, the one who through grace has reached the goal of a good end by obedient service could have fallen through sloth and perished through his own fault. So, walking the middle way with Christ as our guide, we assert the labor of dutiful service after grace, without which we are nothing. But we entirely exclude arrogance and presumption about our labor. We toil with all our strength so that grace may not be made void in us, and we declare that whatever we have received from the Lord's hand is a gift, not a reward. We know that the fruit of that very labor is a matter of duty, not of merit, and we say with the evangelist: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to do.

I have mentioned these points briefly, as a letter requires. Let your Unanimity reply by return whether you accept or reject them. Whoever does not follow this measure of truth, in which grace goes before and effort rises up to meet it, will deserve to be barred from the sacred thresholds. Yet I hold on to your goodness, which is inseparable from me, along the way, embracing it with sincere kindness, and I desire that you remain within the bosom of mother church once you have repudiated this error. If it is rejected quickly, it will seem to have been ignorance; but if it is stubbornly defended, it will be counted as blasphemy. For we turn grave blame back upon the Author himself if we say that he was unwilling to give the one who perished the possibility of attaining salvation [at least anyone already capable of exercising free choice], since we cannot possibly deny that he will condemn the transgressor of his commandment when he examines him in judgment. If someone is not answerable for what he received, I do not see how he can be guilty for what he lost. And so we would sin against God: having first asserted his grace too incautiously, we would end up appearing to attack his justice.

I am keeping a copy of this letter with me, to be produced in the assembly of the holy bishops if need be. If your Fraternity thinks it should be accepted, let him promptly send it back signed with his own hand, or else reply in a later letter that he rejects it entirely. But if you are unwilling to send it back signed, as I said, your very silence will prove that you still openly persist in error, and you will thereby leave me no choice but to expose you in public assemblies. So reply on the basis of what I have sent you, and say without evasion whether you acknowledge these things or reject them.

[I, Auxanius, bishop in the name of Christ, have reread it; and I, Faustus, have reread the copy of my letter; and I, Paul, bishop in the name of Christ, have reread it; and Eutropius, bishop in the name of Christ; Pragmatius, bishop in the sign of Christ; Patiens, bishop in Christ; I, Euphronius, have reread it and admired its holy fullness; I, Megethius, bishop, have reread it; and I, Eutropius, bishop in the name of Christ, have reread it; and I, Leucadius, bishop in the name of Christ, have reread it; and Julian, bishop in the name of Christ; Lucidus the priest.] Likewise, in another hand: I, Faustus, have reread the copy of my letter and signed it.
II. COPY OF THE LETTER OF LUCIDUS THE PRIEST.

TO MY MOST BLESSED LORDS AND MOST REVEREND FATHERS IN CHRIST, THE BISHOPS EUPHRONIUS, LEONTIUS, FONTEIUS, VIVENTIUS, MAMERTUS, PATIENS, VERIANUS, AUXANIUS, FAUSTUS, PAUL, MEGETHIUS, GRAECUS, EUTROPIUS, LEONTIUS, CLAUDIUS, MARCELLUS, CROCUS, BASIL, CLAUDIUS, URSICINUS, PRAETEXTATUS, PRAGMATIUS, THEOPLASTUS, LEUCADIUS, VIVENTIUS, JULIAN, AMICALIS, JOHN, OPILIO AND LICINIUS, LUCIDUS THE PRIEST.

Your correction brings salvation to all, and your judgment is medicine. So I too consider it the best remedy to excuse my past errors by accusing them, and to cleanse myself by a saving profession of faith.

Accordingly, in keeping with the recent decrees of the praiseworthy council, I join you in condemning the view that says the labor of human obedience is not to be joined to divine grace; that says that after the first man's fall the will's freedom of choice was entirely extinguished; that says that Christ our Lord and Savior did not undergo death for the salvation of all; that says that God's foreknowledge forcibly drives man to death, or that those who perish perish by God's will; that says that anyone who sins after lawfully receiving baptism dies in Adam; that says that some are consigned to death and others predestined to life; that says that from Adam to Christ none of the gentiles were saved by God's first grace, that is, by the law of nature, in view of Christ's coming, because all had lost free choice in the first parent; that says that the patriarchs and prophets, or all the greatest of the saints, dwelt in paradise even before the time of redemption; that says that there are no fires and no hell. All these I condemn as impious and full of sacrilege.

I assert God's grace in such a way that I always join human striving and effort to grace. I declare that the freedom of the human will has not been extinguished but weakened and enfeebled, that the one who is saved is still in danger, and that the one who perished could have been saved. I also declare that Christ, our God and Savior, as far as the riches of his goodness are concerned, offered the price of his death for all, and that he wills no one to perish, since he is the Savior of all people, especially of believers, and is rich toward all who call on him. And since in matters so weighty conscience must be satisfied, I recall that I said earlier that Christ came only for those whom he foreknew would believe. I was following the Lord's sayings, in which he says: Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many; and this: This is the cup of my blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins; and also the apostle's saying: Just as it is appointed for men to die once, so Christ too was offered once to take away the sins of many.

But now the truth has been made plain to me by the authority of the sacred testimonies, which are found in abundance throughout the divine scriptures, and by the reasoning of the elders' teaching. I gladly confess that Christ came for the lost as well, since they perished against his will. It is not right to confine the riches of his immense goodness and his divine benefits to those alone who appear to be saved. If we say that Christ brought remedies only to those who have been redeemed, we will seem to acquit the unredeemed, who clearly must be punished for having despised redemption.

I also assert that, according to the plan and order of the ages, some were saved by the law of grace, others by the law of Moses, and others by the law of nature, which God wrote in the hearts of all, in hope of Christ's coming. Yet none, from the beginning of the world, was released from the bond of original sin except through the intercession of the sacred blood. I also profess that eternal fires and the flames of hell have been prepared for capital sins, since the divine sentence rightly follows human sins that persist to the end. Those who have not believed these things with their whole heart justly incur that sentence. Pray for me, holy lords and apostolic fathers.
I, Lucidus the priest, have signed this letter with my own hand. I affirm what is asserted in it and condemn what is condemned.
III. LETTER OF FAUSTUS.

You ask me, most reverend of priests, how we should answer the Arians, who with blasphemous mouths try to assert: "It cannot be," they say, "that the begotten is anything but younger than the unbegotten." In reply, as though ordered to break my silence completely, I shall venture an answer, not so much to teach the subject as to confess the faith. My first concern is not to wrap things already obscure in a laboured, polished style. Instead I shall set out some signs of my poor understanding, meant to serve comprehension rather than ornament. I answer, then, as disciples usually answer the masters who question them. So I speak at the command of your Beatitude so that I may be examined, and I admit my lack of skill so that I may be taught. For if I keep silent before a man of great learning, I can hardly find out what I do not know.
Since we are about to speak of the unbegotten, we must know that the substances of things are one matter and the names of things another. For example, when you have said "gold"

and "silver," you have not at once produced the metal itself, only the names of the metal. Gold as a particular kind of thing is one matter, and gold as a word in speech is another. Naming it is one thing, and holding it is another.

"Begotten" and "unbegotten" signify the Godhead; they are not the Godhead itself. They name the nature; they are not the nature. The terms "unbegotten" and "begotten" serve to let you understand who subsists from whom, and to recognize that the Father is not from the Son but the Son from the Father. Beginning from beginning is both one and without a beginning, just as you might say "God from God," and yet there are not two gods but one God. "Begotten," then, and "unbegotten," and "proceeding from both" point to persons, not natures. For the majesty that belongs to the Father without division from the Son and the Holy Spirit can be distinguished by names, but it cannot be ranked in degrees.

At this point, now that you have been warned, you must give the matter your full attention. Perhaps you will say: "Because he is from him, he comes after him." Come, let us feed our understanding on this point with some comparisons. Let us see whether one thing can arise from another and yet not be later in age than the thing it arises from. For example, the very name "son" is believed to derive from the name "father," and yet it is not found to be later, because unless the son were born, the father would not be called father. Here is a name exactly as old as the name it comes from. Although the son is from the father, it is the son who gives the father his name. The person who is born gains for the one who begets him the title of a father's love. Though the one comes from the other, the one is not shown to be later nor the other older. Again, the Son is called the "arm" because of the power of his works. See: the arm proceeds from the body, and yet the body is not older than the arm. A word is uttered from the voice, and yet, though it is born from the mouth,

it is not shown to be later than the voice. Fire and heat are inseparable partners. Heat is understood without doubt to come from fire, and yet fire is by no means recognized as prior to its own heat. Here, then, is a thing that seems to arise from another and yet is joined to its source with no interval of time between them.

When we come to God, however, "begotten" is like "just" and "justice," "wise" and "wisdom," "merciful" and "mercy." We understand, following the Apostle, that justice and wisdom arise directly from the just and wise God. And just as he was never just without justice or wise without wisdom, so the Son is from the Father, but the Father could never have been without the Son.

No doubt the Arians do not dare to deny our Savior. But by calling him lesser they lose the ability to assert that he is God. For God by nature subsists in the dignity of fullness, and their impiety testifies by its first confession that it worships one God. But by making him younger than the one thought to be older, it makes two and cuts through the solid unity. For the very word "lesser" points to another who is greater than he. Yet who is older than he who declares of himself, "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last"? When the Jews asked him who he was, he answered, "The beginning, who am also speaking to you." Through the prophet he confirms with truthful voice, "Before me there was no god, and after me there will be none." If the Father says this, he confirms that no inferior began after him; if the Son says it, he declares that the Father was in no way before him. The prophetic word clearly points to him: "This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him," and after this: "He was seen among men and lived among men." According to these texts, then, between begotten and unbegotten there is no rank, because he is one. No time comes between them, because he is first. He is not to be placed second, because he is alone. He is not to be called lesser, because he is full. He is therefore the one God, perfect and of simple nature, beyond all reckoning and incapable of suffering, even though we confess, truly and for our salvation, that according to the flesh he suffered for us.

After this, as your next question, you ask me how, with regard to the substance of God, a certain letter could say: "He felt nothing with the sensation of one who suffers, but he felt with the feeling of one who suffers with others."

First, it is very easy to see, and even the philosophers knew it, that in man the various affections, namely justice, mercy, holiness, benevolence and devotion, are things added from outside, and that is why they are called affections. God, however, is not affected by them in a way that involves suffering, because they are known to be in him permanently and by nature. So what in man is affection and grace is in God power and nature. As for the saying, "He felt nothing with the sensation of one who suffers, but he felt with the feeling of one who suffers with others," why should anyone hesitate to say it in the same sense that the prophetic word also uses: "Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chasten me in your fury"; and, "The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent"; and again, "The Lord was angry with his people and abhorred his inheritance"? Likewise, with contrasting feelings, he is described as having loved Jacob and hated Esau. He is said to be grieved at our sins and to rejoice in his works, and, as one subject to feelings, he says of himself, "I repent that I made man." From the highest seat of heaven he declares, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" He also seems to show the feeling of one who suffers with others when he says, "I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink," and other sayings of this kind that come readily to mind.

Picture a priest who knows many languages and stands among different peoples. To instruct a Hebrew in Hebrew, a Greek in Greek and a Roman in Latin, he shapes his words to each one's understanding and fits his speech to each one's mind, dividing the different sounds of one heart and breast among varied listeners. In the same way God, when he is about to speak with man, deigns to take up man's language, since he was also to take up human form. Through sounds our minds can grasp, he expresses feelings in our own manner. When he describes the functions of the five human senses, he says, "The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers"; and again, "The mouth of the Lord has spoken"; likewise, "And he smelled the sweet odor"; and, "My hand made all these things. Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet." In this way he conveys to our hearts the workings of things by referring to his own members. Hence, because of his inexpressible condescension toward the human race, which does not disdain to call servants his friends and sons and to address them so, man in turn converses with him in human speech and in human fashion.

For the rest, God's anger is justice, God's fury is the vigor of severity, God's swearing is his decreeing, and God's repenting is a sentence, though one often changed. And when he says he is harmed by someone persecuting him, he shows the guilt of the one who does the harm. If these exchanges of human speech are taken away, we are entirely cut off from the ministry of speech and from every means by which God is either understood or proclaimed. Why then, among such sayings, can it not be said, "but he felt with the feeling of one who suffers with others"?

If, then, a simple and open answer has satisfied the master who examines me, let us pass to the third question, which you bid me answer: what in human affairs is to be considered corporeal and what incorporeal. On this I shall set out some points, not presuming on my own understanding but following the opinion of the holy elders. I do so all the more because these points cannot harm the mind, can nourish faith, and can arm and rouse us against the perversities of the Arians, to the point where the Son is seen to be equal to the Father.

When the discussion concerns a loftier subject, then, the senses and the mind must be prepared for a subtler understanding. Some of the most learned fathers assert that invisible things are one category and incorporeal things another. They define whatever is created as visible matter, comprehensible to its maker and corporeal. For they assert that the nature of both souls and angels is corporeal, because it is circumscribed by a beginning and by space. So we read in a certain treatise of Saint Jerome: "They suppose," he says, "that the globes of the stars are [?] spirits"; and again: "If angels, and even heavenly bodies, are said to be unclean in comparison with God, what do you think man must be reckoned?" Yet amid all this you deny that the soul is corporeal on the grounds that, in the opinion of some, it is neither in a place nor subsists in quality or quantity, though this, clearly, is to be believed of the majesty of God alone. For we read in a treatise of the fathers that is most widely accepted: "To enter and fill all things," it says, "is possible to the Trinity alone. It so penetrates the whole intellectual nature that it can not only embrace and surround it but also slip into it, and, being incorporeal, be poured into a body. For although we declare that some natures are spiritual, such as angels, archangels and the other powers, as well as our own soul, or indeed this fine air, they are by no means to be considered incorporeal. In their own way they have a body by which they subsist, though one far finer, beyond comparison, than our bodies, according to the statement of the Apostle: 'There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies.'" From these words it is plainly gathered that nothing is incorporeal except God alone, and that therefore to him alone can all spiritual and intellectual substances be penetrable.

Since this is so, you object that the soul is not corporeal because, as was said, it is neither in a place nor subsists in quality or quantity. How dangerous it is to believe this will be shown in what follows. For now, once the matter has been discussed, the whole question of our treatise will turn on this: if the soul is neither in a place nor subject to quantity, let us concede that it is without doubt incorporeal; but if I show that it is bounded by quantity or enclosed in a place, then you yourself will no longer doubt that it is also contained in a body. How can the soul not be in a place, when it is inserted into the limbs and bound to the organs, and, roving only in its movements, is held enclosed by the condition of its substance? But suppose you think the soul should be declared not to be in a place because it roams through different places by its senses and is carried off in its thoughts. Then it must first be understood that the soul's own state is one thing, and the activity of thought born from the soul is another. So we should rather hold that whenever it imagines something, it is busy with its own movements within itself, and whenever it seems to behold something else, that thing is rather being portrayed to it in the mirror of memory. When it thinks of a dear friend who is absent, has it already satisfied its longing as though it had seen him? When, for example, it paints the likeness of Peter or Paul in the secret places of the mind, has it at once entered the inner dwellings of paradise where we know them to be? Or when, after a reading, it has pictured in its heart the damnation of that rich man, has it already gone down to the place of his torments and the depths of hell, which the living cannot reach?

Without doubt, the soul either fashions all these things through various likenesses within the secret places of the breast, or else, if restless thought, driven by a slippery motion, runs about outside the soul's seat, it does this very thing in a place. And whether it thinks of a city or of any region, it is fixed there only by its sense lingering wherever the mind's attention carries it off. It can imagine some things; it cannot embrace all things at once. So when the soul has thought of Alexandria or Jerusalem, if it was truly there with its whole presence, as you suppose, let it describe to us the layout of the places, the faces of the people, and the movements and doings of the crowds. Take this very moment, when we exchange speech with one another by the action of the spirit. I feel that I am speaking with you, but within my own consciousness; I do not feel that I have come to where you are. For if the soul is truly believed to be carried along with its senses, it would be made present in its own person, through its thoughts, to those it remembers. See, at this present moment I think of you and see you with my remembering mind, and yet I am wholly ignorant of what those I remember are doing, whether you are taking your rest or are occupied with reading or prayer. This happens because I reach you by the affection of the heart, not by the actual reality of my substance. For the nature of our soul does not consist in its movements, which we feel to be now the best, now the worst. If it were to be believed that the soul consists of its thoughts, why does it remain in its vigor and liveliness when they sometimes vanish and perish? How many of the countless thoughts and cares in us die, and even to our benefit, and serve rather the freedom of the inner life! If the soul consisted of them, it certainly could not survive their perishing. Hence reason itself tells our consciences rather this: that each soul either brings forth many thoughts conceived within itself from the causes of things, or sends out its senses like officers or servants to be occupied with various needs, while it itself rests in the chamber of its body, which it will leave once and for all.

So, to offer once more a sufficient example that the soul is in a place: was not Lazarus's soul within his body while life lasted? When life withdrew, was it not exiled from its bodily dwelling? And when it was poured back into the lifeless body, did it not return, called back to the place from which it had been absent? You see it driven out of the lodging it lived in and then restored to the lodging from which it had been absent, and do you still contend that it is not in a place? But why speak of corruptible man, when he whose flesh did not see corruption also possessed a soul that was spotless, yet in a place? He certainly had it within himself when he was fastened to the cross, and without doubt he sent it out of himself when he lay in the tomb. How can that not be in a place which the flesh contains, life joins to it, and death separates from it? But if, as you say, the nature of souls is not subject to the constraint of place, then are not even those souls shut up in the prison of hell present in the region of paradise as well? Tell me, I ask you, if they are not in a place, how does that vast chasm, set grimly between them, separate sinners from the company and fellowship of the righteous, so that they can neither go from here to there nor cross from there to here? It is already perfectly clear that whatever is contained by space is circumscribed by quantity. If you have acknowledged that the soul is in a place, concede that it is corporeal. Tell me, did not the very soul of our glorious Redeemer leave the world when he ascended to heaven?

For my part, I would not doubt that even angels are in a place. It is certain that they are now contained in heaven, now carried through the empty air, now sent down to earth. The divine word describes them ascending and descending in the patriarch's vision, and if they were not in a place but everywhere, they certainly could not come and go by ascending and descending. The most blessed Gabriel himself testifies that he stands before the Lord. Yet when he announced that the Lord of heaven was to be poured into Mary's womb, and when he stood before the eyes of the Lord's mother, he was without doubt absent from heaven. He was not flying over the seas or filling the empty, outspread expanses of the vast air, but occupied only the place where he was present. This being so, whatever occupies a place is a body. And I do not see how anyone can escape the law of place who is sent from place to place and, like a body, is moved by motion and approach, descends by his mass, runs about by his mobility, goes, returns, departs and ascends. That other one too, I suppose, is in a place, since he has not been in heaven from the moment he was cast out of heaven. And he did not show himself alone to be in a place, for when he was hurled down from on high he dragged a third of the stars with him. Tell me, if he has no body, what fell in that casting down? Why do you deny him a bodily nature when you dare not deny his fall? And if, as you say, he has no body, he will not burn. But where, if not in a body, will he feel the fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels? It is superfluous, I think, to say that through his dwelling in this air he acquired a certain density from the compacting of the elements. Tell me, if he had no body, where in the air could there be any compacting, where could this nameless density gather itself, unless he brought something bodily down with him from that heavenly citadel? As I see it, he would be carrying a borrowed body to his torments. So recognize, even from your own claim, that he is a body. A body is that which is stained, which is spotted, which is corrupted by anything added to it from outside.

This one, then, once the firstborn of the angels, has now become the prince of darkness. As though corporeal, he was beautiful before and is now degenerate; once he shone with heavenly splendor, now he is fouled with the hideous horror of hellish sin. That, I say, is a body which is driven from its dwelling, circumscribed by quantity, changed in quality and consumed by pain. Since this is so, see into what deep guilt those plunge themselves who call the soul incorporeal. First, since God, the author of the universe, is said to have made all things in number and weight, the soul would then be believed exempt from the matter of all creation. If it is neither corporeal nor in a place, and if it is not contained by place, then it is diffused everywhere and is said to enter and fill all things and to be present everywhere. As though the creature were made a partner of its creator and frailty of its author, it is joined to him, to be counted no longer a work of God but a part of God. See where the slide into deep error leads those who assert it! It is true that the things above you are invisible to us. But to him all things are comprehensible, and just so they are corporeal; for he made all things from nothing, and as he established them by his work, so he gave them body in matter. Among all things, the soul too is counted, and just as he allotted them weight, number and measure, so he also set their quantity.

Meanwhile, someone may perhaps think it should be asserted, as was said, that the fine angelic nature, having picked up a certain contamination by mixing with this air, will be found liable to the flames. Then, as he says, if what will burn is made of air, the punishment will rage only in the air, not in the angel himself but outside him. But without doubt the force of pain can rule nowhere except in the substance of a body. See where this rash and ignorant conviction leads! When it speaks of the incorporeal, it also professes the incomprehensible. In this way it ascribes to the created work what belongs to the Creator alone, shares the privileges of majesty with created things, and stretches an undue power in the thing made to the point of insulting the Maker. If we inquire carefully into the outcome to which you would direct the mind, it was above all this belief that rolled the devil down from his station in that blessed seat. For this he lost the dignity of an angel, when he presumed that he had the nature of God.

There is therefore one God who is incorporeal, because he is both incomprehensible and diffused everywhere, for he took no material beginning from the matter of any bodily making. And therefore the Son is coeternal with the Father. Made by no work and circumscribed by no beginnings, he pervades with incorporeal majesty all the things he fashioned within the body of the world, which are comprehensible and corporeal to him as their potter. Begotten from the unbegotten, that is, from the Father, yet always with the Father, in the undivided fellowship of the Holy Spirit, he rules over the things he called forth from nothing. Amen.
4. To my lord, my father and patron alike, Pope Faustus, from Paulinus.

Fear holds me back from writing to you, while affection drives me to it, and between the two my mind is tossed about in uncertainty, like a reckless sailor who trusts his sails to doubtful fortune. But since I have a sure harbour in you, I often take on myself the outcome of an uncertain voyage. Even so, I have chosen to risk wearying you rather than to incur guilt, for I know very well that my lord Faustus receives my letters without disdain. But my lord Marinus the hermit, a holy man whose extreme strictness makes him one to be feared, has struck such fear into me with his great severity that I come to you with questions. I am entangled in sins of the flesh, and I commit everything a guilty man can. If, when I come to complete the day of our human lot, I obtain a sudden penance, I wish to know whether it removes my sin in part or wholly. Or are those who believe in the united Trinity, and do not sin in spirit, tormented for all their bodily vices with everlasting punishments and tortures, with flames and torments?

My own opinion is that, if a Christian is to suffer all these things, an Arian could suffer nothing more. I also ask whether the soul, once separated from the bond of the body, is consigned to some kind of custody, or kept shut up in a prison, or tossed about uncertainly among the breezes. And since I know that in that hour every thought perishes, I respectfully ask, if you will allow it, whether thought, both good and bad, departs from the soul, which is shown to be immortal, or whether some sense and understanding is kept, and whether it feels anything of honourable affection. We know that everything is granted to the good, so that after death they can bestow even greater benefits on the living; let me learn what is either given to the wicked or taken from them. Let me be taught whether the soul itself is better understood [?] as corporeal or incorporeal. And since the flesh is weak but the spirit is willing, I long in my ignorance to know what share in sin the soul incurs for a bodily error, and how something immortal is tormented for mortal vices. Likewise, let me learn whether soul and spirit are the same, or how they are to be distinguished.

For the man I mentioned, even binding his words with an oath, has terrified me by saying that whoever gives way to bodily vices can earn no pardon. Instead, he said, such a person is kept in these same punishments at the very resurrection, and cannot expiate by the torments of hell what (life) had contracted when hardened by bodily vices. Yet, most wretched as I am, I believe this: whoever has never broken the sign of the divine name, once received, or the mark of our Lord fixed on his forehead, and has never been conscious of malice or a deceitful falsifier, will undergo light torments to expiate his error, and when that day is spent he will bring forth a pure airy sense and the fire of a simple soul. For if we sinners are to suffer all the things my lord Marinus threatens, I do not know what more the ungodly could deserve. Forgive me for troubling your piety in this way, as I long to be taught by a veteran master, I who hope one day to be his new disciple.
V. FAUSTUS TO PAULINUS, HIS SON, A DISTINGUISHED LORD, WHO DESERVES MY SPECIAL AND HIGHEST HONOUR.

The pages of your letters have always been admirable to me, but this one shone more brightly than ever with the twin light of eloquence and faith, as it asks about the state of the soul and sighs with anxious fear over the judgements to come. The divine word says in one place: To one who asks rightly, wisdom
will be credited. For knowing what you do not know is itself a part of knowledge, and so is asking prudently about what your ignorance keeps you from understanding.

Your first question was whether, under the pressure of the final extremity, a momentary penance can wipe out capital offences. A person deceives himself with a persuasion hostile to his own good if he thinks that stains contracted over a long life can be removed by sudden and by then useless groans. At that time there can be confession, but there cannot be satisfaction. God is not mocked, and so a man deceives himself if he has lived for death through many years and then, already half-dead, rises to seek life. He wants to look dutiful at the very moment when every service of body and soul is being withdrawn from the Lord's service. In securing the health of the inner man, what is expected is not only the will to receive the remedy but the useful work of carrying it out. For so we read: If, it says, the sinner does penance for his sins (it says "does," not merely "receives"), he shall live in the righteousness he has wrought. You see that this kind of medicine must be asked for with the mouth and completed by deeds. A man seems to insult God if he refused to come to the physician when he could, and now begins to want to come when he cannot. So the devotion we bring to healing our wounds must be as great as the intent of the mind that was so headlong and so vigorous for evil when we sinned.

Your second question was whether faith alone, and knowledge of the united Trinity, is enough for salvation. In divine matters what is required is not only a reason for believing but a reason for pleasing God. Faith stripped of merits is therefore empty and void, as the apostle says: What use is it if someone says he has faith but has no works? Can faith save him? He goes on to say: Faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself. But someone will say: You have faith and I have works. Show me your faith without works, and I will show you my faith by my works. By these words, belief by itself is shown not to be enough. Even the devil is found to know God and believe, as the same apostle says: You believe that God is one; you do well. The demons also believe, and tremble. Do you want to know, you empty man, that faith without works is dead? Was not Abraham our father justified by works? And so that we should not place our hope in faith alone, he concluded: For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead; without works, he said, a man is empty. For the sake of brevity we leave out many similar testimonies. Did the apostle Paul, from whose heart the Lord spoke as from his own temple, judge that faith alone could suffice him to overcome the evils of the world? He says: I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected. See, he feared to become rejected through the vices of the body. Though already approved, he dreaded becoming a vessel of dishonour through the deadly contagion of carnal passions, he who had already been made a chosen vessel.

Let us see whether faith alone defends a man who squanders his life, and whether, as you say, the baptized can no longer perish. I recognize how carnal evils make a man a stranger to God and a slave of obscene pleasures. The apostle says to the Galatians: The works of the flesh are plain: fornication, impurity, licentiousness, murders, drunkenness, carousing and the like; those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God. And to the Ephesians: No fornicator or impure or greedy person, which is the service of idols, will have an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. He calls it the service of idols because when anything is loved with the desire with which God ought to be loved, such affection is likened to idols. Such a man is without doubt shut out of the kingdom and handed over to hell and death. And it is plain that many baptized people, though their faith is intact, perish for ever in various ways. The divine word condemns not those who transgress the faith, nor those who violate baptism, but those who neglected to be merciful, when it says: Judgement without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy. And again: I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me nothing to drink, I was a stranger and you did not take me in, naked and you did not clothe me. If the company of the flock on the left had not known the gift of baptism, he would first have charged them with unbelief and ungodliness. But though they were baptized, he assigns them to death because they were empty of good works, and abandons them to everlasting flames. He concludes the severity of his sentence in this way: Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels. And again: He will gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire. Likewise: These, he says, will go into eternal life, but those into eternal fire. Amid all this, let each person take care not to accuse God of lying about his promise of reward by doubting the eternity of punishment. It is not so, for he who knows how to honour merits knows how to punish sins. These three capital sins, then, sacrilege, adultery and murder, will burn there in everlasting fires unless they have been expiated here by the remedies of a complete penance. We do not read that these merciless people turned away from faith and baptism, but we learn on divine authority that they earned perpetual death.

Your concern, looking providently to the future, also prompts you to ask whether souls, when they put off the body, put off with it the power of feeling and understanding and their affection. Let us question that rich man in the gospel. He is not wandering among the breezes, as the ravings of the poets claim, but is placed in the prison of hell, among those who are shut in awaiting punishment, amid the flames of conscience before the day of judgement. Anxious that his brothers, who were still in this world, should amend their lives, he earnestly pleaded and spoke with Abraham across the vast chasm set between them. Stirred by a lively memory of his brothers, he made this plea for the living: I beg you, I say, father Abraham, to send Lazarus to my father's house, for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torment; and if someone goes to them from the dead, they will do penance. See, though he is imprisoned in the dungeon of hell and has no remedy left for himself, he still keeps his old affection for his own. And when a damned man pleads for sinners, he shows how great a concern the righteous, who are refreshed amid the groves of paradise, have for the good of those dear to them.

You ask what is either given to the wicked or taken from them after the end. Of the wicked we read: The desire of sinners shall perish. Once their craving for earthly things and their ambition for honours have been removed, only the weight of rendering an account and the fear of an unbearable examination will hang over them. Their senses will not be taken away; rather, they will be made freer and keener for thinking about the other world.

You ask to be taught whether the soul itself is corporeal or incorporeal. Know, then, that only that which is not enclosed by time nor confined by the limits of place, which belongs to God alone, is incorporeal. One eminent teacher, when someone asked him where God was, replied: God is not somewhere. What is somewhere is contained in a place, and what is contained in a place is a body. This being so, all flesh is body, but not all body is flesh. [And since not only the soul but also the invisible and heavenly substance of the angels is contained in local spaces, it is shown to be corporeal and comprehensible to its Creator. For what is the thing that was thrust down from the heavenly seats and gave up its place, if not something corporeal? What is it that felt the fall? What is it that is being made ready for punishment, liable to eternal flame? Blessed Lazarus too, after the tongues of the dogs that served him, was received into the hands of angels. Of him we read: It came to pass that the beggar died and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom. He showed that his soul was corporeal when it was carried by the ministry of angels into Abraham's bosom, that is, into a remote and blessed retreat. And the holy prophet says of his own soul: Lead my soul, O Lord, out of prison, that is, out of the narrow confines of its bodily lodging. Hence, by reason of its created nature, the soul, which can be wounded by the darts of sin or, changed in its qualities, raised even to the glory of the divine image, is plainly and beyond doubt shown to be corporeal in relation both to God and to the angels, by whom it can be grasped and carried from place to place.

Here we must also ask why it is that, when both men, that is, soul and body, sinned together in the region of paradise at the devil's persuasion, the flesh alone received the penalty for the transgression through the condition of death, so that a shared guilt ended in the punishment of only one. We must understand that death did not reach the soul because the Lord placed his image and likeness in it. For as God is immortal, merciful, just and patient, so he pours the gifts of these virtues into the face of our inner man, so that the more patient, the more just, the more merciful a person became, the more he would appear endowed with the gift of sharing in the divine nature. As the apostle says: Christ dwells in the inner man through faith.

You also ask why the soul should share with its flesh in some way in a bodily error. Original sin embraces both because they are united in one bodily lodging, and both (men) are bound in the same way in fellowship of sin. In the same way they have one case to answer for their share in crimes, just as they will share equal glory in the reward of virtues. The outer man would never fall into the abyss of lust unless the inner man gave it consent. Let us question ourselves, and we will be able to recognize within ourselves that the mind as mistress exercises command and the flesh as its subject renders service: the one supplies the labour, the other the counsel. Obedience would cease in the servant if the will had not first gone ahead in the one who commands. So those who, on the contrary, will rejoice together in the reward must recognize that they share a like condition in damnation.

You go on to ask how something immortal can be tormented for mortal vices. Evils are indeed mortal, but the torment of evils will be immortal, and the crosses of sins will remain when the vices themselves have ceased. The lower substance will carry the better one with it to judgement, just as an admixture of lead forces gold into the smelting fire. So for mortal evils a man will die to God and live to hell. This will be the death there: that one is not allowed to die in one's pain.

Your concern extends also to whether soul and spirit are the same, or how they are to be distinguished. We know that there are only two substances in man, namely soul and body. Spirit, however, is sometimes shown to be part of our nature and sometimes found to be something added. Sometimes "spirit" is used for the soul; sometimes it is understood as the longing for virtue and a spiritual disposition. In this way one and the same person is now carnal, now animal, and now spiritual too. The carnal are those of whom the Lord says: My spirit shall not remain in these men, for they are flesh; and the apostle: Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. A man is carnal when he serves his belly and throat by excess in eating and drinking and makes the good of life consist in gluttony and greed. But a man becomes animal when, still thinking little of God, he is moved by worldly prudence, according to the soul, to provide for various things; when he delights either in investigating the causes of hidden things out of idle curiosity or in philosophical studies. Hence the apostle says: The animal man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God. But he begins to be spiritual when he longs for what is honourable, holy and spiritual; when he rises with vigour of heart to the worship of divine fear; when he invites the Holy Spirit to himself through purity of body and the guarding of chastity, so that the apostle's words can be said of him: You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you. These things are not implanted in man by nature, but are joined to him by grace in such a way that they can be separated through guilt when sloth intervenes. Hence the same apostle says: But whoever violates the temple of God, God will destroy him. See: through faith such a person is seen to be not only baptized but even the temple of God, and yet for various shameful deeds he will be destroyed by God's severity. We should understand that the word "destruction" here means the eternal ruin of a lost soul. Those who are called members of Christ are beyond doubt counted among the baptized, and yet see how they are compared to the lost, how by the working of shameful deeds they fall away from the nobility of sons, as the apostle says: Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a harlot? Those too had most clearly received the gifts of the second birth who were even powerful in a variety of spiritual gifts. Of them the Lord says in the gospel: Many will say to me on that day, Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name? And then I will declare to them: I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity. Who would not understand that those who are ordered to depart from the Father's sight have been cut off from salvation? Death will undoubtedly receive as its portion those whom Life, which is Christ, did not know. Do you doubt that the baptized are handed over to destruction for their iniquities, when you know that baptism itself is lost through crimes of many kinds?

Your letter, as the page shows, borrowed from the poet and supposed the soul to be a fire of simple air. That can rightly be said only of the substance of the Godhead, to which it is agreed that nothing has been added, nothing conferred by a higher power, nothing joined. God is both just and justice, living and life, wise and wisdom, power and the source of powers. In his chief goods he himself is what he possesses. But man must be understood as twofold: he can be called living and just and wise, but cannot be called life and justice and wisdom, because he is clothed with these in such a way that he is sometimes stripped of them. What is given to man is inherent in God. Man, for example, is gilded; God is gold, and in him power and grace are the same as his nature. As for your subtle remark, "If sinners are to suffer all the things my lord Marinus threatens, I do not know what more the ungodly could deserve": even among everlasting evils the punishments have their degrees. So one guilty of grave sins is tormented with torments that, though endless, are somehow bearable, while the ungodly man is tormented with unheard-of tortures. The grace of baptism could indeed rescue a man from eternal death, were it not that in some people its integrity and dignity are lost. It is a grave crime that the heretic was unwilling to receive it, but it is no less grave that a Christian both received it and lost it. For the man who, trusting in his baptism, burst into the wedding feast and violated that sacred assembly lost the brightness of purity, was expelled from the illustrious gathering of the righteous, and was thrust out into the outer darkness. Are we to believe that a man possesses the snowy whiteness of holy regeneration if he is incestuous, a poisoner and a man of blood, or if he cuts short his life by a fall or by hanging and passes over to the company of the ungodly?

We read that unquenchable flames are prepared for capital deeds, but we do not read that a man living in his evils is saved by baptism alone. It is dangerous for a hostile sense of security to promise itself what heavenly Scripture does not say; it is far more dangerous for it not to believe what the Truth threatens. You say that the most blessed Marinus spoke about certain things with threats. But just as what the Lord has promised to those who love him has not entered into the heart of man, as the apostle also testifies, because of its greatness, so the immensity of the torments to come exceeds the narrow limits of the human mind. These are evils that the shadow of a momentary penance does not remove, that faith without works does not drive back, and to which the course of the passing ages will be unable to set an end in the unquenchable flames. Amid their inexhaustible vapours the soul will, too late, both feel and see itself to be corporeal. So let us forestall the last day with righteous, pious and chaste works, and by fearing here what it will be useless to fear there, let us avoid it. Let us put an end here to endless contritions, and by thinking now, to our salvation, of fires that cannot be endured, let us win for ourselves from those very fires an eternal refreshment.

I am sure of your faith, and that the saving testimonies of sincere truth will be more welcome to you than the decked-out polish of studied speech. With a father's affection we send greetings to my son Eminentius, our sweet glory. May our Lord fill your Magnificence, so admirable to me, with present goods and make it worthy of eternal ones.
VI. FAUSTUS TO FELIX, A MOST PIOUS LORD WHO DESERVES SPECIAL SERVICES, MY BROTHER FOR EVER, AS I TRUST, AND MY LORD IN ALL THINGS.

It is great evidence of devotion and faith that across the vast distances of such wide regions, and through so many dangers that lie between, you extend the breadth of your love all the way to us. In this exile of ours the skilful mercy of our God performs a twofold office: with fatherly care it scours away our rust, and it brings to light your faith toward us and proves your devotion. With kindly skill it files us down and brings you forward; it narrows us for our good and enlarges you; we are rebuked, you advance. Our losses pass over into your gains. Though you are our creditors, you begin to be our debtors, since we are the cause of your devotion and the material of your reward. Your works draw profit from us; your merits borrow increase from our scourges. The affection of your care reaches us, its fruit reaches God, and so in a double way, both by our chastisement and by your recompense, we are bound by divine benefits. Indeed, the completeness of your consolation had almost imposed silence on me rather than a reply. For your very eagerness to ask is already a pattern of living, which you draw in full measure every day from the effective teaching and the living example of my lord, your father, the holy bishop Leontius. Yet I am not surprised if you also ask, though it is superfluous, about my own rule of life, since you know my singular affection for you. You believe that my teaching is as perfect an aid to your faith as you would wish it to be; but although my speech, made slower still by my present illness, can hardly satisfy your ardour, I will nevertheless in a few words not so much instruct your way of life as remind you of it.

Recognition of sin, fear of judgement and terror of eternal fire give great instruction to those who are earnest. So for offering the sacrifices of prayer the silence of the night is a friend to those who make use of it; let it be followed by moderate reading until the third hour, so that spiritual exercise may never cease to be desired and may always grow. Would that the Lord might provide you with even two faithful companions with whom to carry out the offices of day and night, and that you might enjoy the attentions of visitors on just two days a week. These are hard things that I speak of, in keeping with the fervour of the one who asks; but may that kind helper of those who labour make his yoke as light for you as his reward will be pleasant. So, if your still timid beginnings allow a little more, let the winter days be spent fasting on alternate days; and these fasts, just as they must be kept in moderation, must also be doubled.

Doubled, I say. For there are two kinds of abstinence. The first is to restrain the appetite of incontinence from food and drink and from the various enticements of fleshly pleasures; to tame the earth of the outward man with the ploughshare of the cross; to serve need rather than pleasure with tempered moderation; and, if weakness allows, to take a meal only on alternate days, until the force of long habit is gradually unlearned. As for clothing, let your dignity lower itself little by little to humbler things, so that the very novelty of sudden plainness may not give offence. For care must be taken that pride is not born even from excessive humility, and vice from virtue. This, however, will easily be overcome if the shameful history of your former way of life is brought before your eyes and a guilty conscience is set before your trembling senses. So it will come about that, while the presumption injected by the devil is chastised by the memory of past evils, and boasting is beaten and driven off by the strong weapons of our faults, the crimes that had begotten death begin to fight for salvation, offences serve as a remedy, medicine is drawn from wounds, and, as the apostle said, we labour to condemn sin by means of sin.

The other kind of abstinence is far loftier and far more precious: to govern the movements of the soul; to bring under the mind's command the irrational disturbances and the rebellious tumults of thoughts struggling against one another; to spit out the poison of malice from the inner recesses of the heart like some deadly sorcery; to steer the soul with the helm of constancy against the waves of various temptations; to join battle, with the authority of an angry faith, against hidden passions as against enemies within one's own household; to drive vain cares far away and abstain from the harmful conversations and desires on which the devil feeds; and through gentleness, patience and calm to cultivate the image of God in the face of the inner man. Then sadness will not break the man who thinks on spiritual and divine things, nor will joy unman him, and an even greatness of spirit will show a heart made firm in the fear of God, so that the noble opening of that book may be applied to us as well: "There was a man, one man, who kept himself from every evil thing." "A man," it says, "one man": that is, always the same, because there was nothing doubtful in him, nothing double, nothing incidental, nothing changeable, nothing at odds with itself. As he remained in the state of his virtues with steady order, the times did not change him, nor did contrary blasts of wind turn him this way and that, as they do the waves of the sea. So too let the earnest servant of God, founded on the unshaken mass of faith, be changed, with Christ working in him, in this one respect only: that he is always putting on new virtues.

Above all, as far as we can with God's help, let us defeat within ourselves those enticements of the five senses. For whatever is lovely to the sight, whatever allures the smell, whatever is soft to the touch, whatever is sweet to the taste, whatever charms the hearing, all of these, if we misuse them, drag our attention down from spiritual things to earthly ones. And so, just as Abraham, the father of faith, conquered those five kings with three hundred and eighteen men, by a mystery hidden in the letters, let us too fight against these chief captains of the vices in the name of Jesus and by the sign of the cross (for that is what the two numerals express), so that we may deserve to hear from the Lord: "To the one who conquers I will give the crown of life"; and: "Whoever conquers will not be harmed by the second death"; and: "The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it." For the soul must do violence to itself, to subject fleshly affections to the spirit, to prefer the cross to delights, to put vigils before sweet sleep, to conquer the adversary in its own members, so that, becoming another person instead of the one it was, it may be found fit for that command of the Lord: "If anyone," he says, "wishes to come after me, let him deny himself." If someone becomes patient instead of wrathful, chaste instead of lustful, gentle instead of bloodthirsty, kind instead of envious, generous instead of greedy: as often as we turn ourselves toward better things, so often do we deny ourselves. And so, that we may rise up to what we ought to be, let us first strive to hate what we were. Whoever hopes to be changed there into glory must first be changed here into life.
VII. TO HIS HOLY LORD AND BROTHER, MOST CLOSELY BOUND TO HIM IN CHRIST, GRAECUS THE DEACON, FROM FAUSTUS.

Honoured by your attention, honoured by your esteem, and moved by affection, I will speak with you in sincere humility, in kindly frankness, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth. You might well have given me reason to keep silent, since with a kind and overly trusting mind you credit me with almost as much skill and learning as yourself; yet by your eagerness to ask you have laid on me the necessity of answering. I feel that I must converse with you in your absence not without trepidation, for on matters so profound, beyond both my powers and yours, there is no less danger in answering than in entrusting great mysteries to an unpolished pen; and so I ought rather to have rebuked my dear friend by silence for what he has put forward too rashly. But in seeking counsel on so great a matter, in which you have strayed far from the royal road, you ought to have asked some men of proven knowledge, senior in learning and in age, whom you could more readily believe, according to the prophetic saying: "Ask your father and he will tell you, your elders and they will say to you." Yet without doubt whoever seeks a guide of any kind wishes to turn aside from error. Furthermore, in what we do or say, and above all in what we presume to commit to writing, we ought to look for fruit and profit from the work. But in this little piece of writing which you were good enough to send me, there appears no eloquence, no knowledge, no reasoning, no edification such as an orderly or heartfelt discourse would give; instead, proof-texts heaped together in utter confusion, just as they came easily to memory, betray the rashness of an incautious heart. The Lord knows that I say these things in astonishment and out of concern for your salvation; so may your asking and my answering serve the common good.

Even if something in the writings of the holy bishop Augustine is thought suspect by very learned men, you should know that nothing among the things you have judged worthy of condemnation has been censured. Rather, you should know that the sense of the faith, especially concerning the two substances or natures, of God and of man, in our Lord and Redeemer, has not only been received in the catholic Church on the authority of the fathers but has also been consecrated by the oracles of the apostles. Accordingly, this word which you say came to you in prophetic fashion (certainly not by the Spirit of God) is gravely damnable before God and before men, unless you first condemn it yourself. Therefore, passing over other points, I will bind up in a brief discourse, as far as I can at a distance, this double error, born of heresy and dragging one into the dangers of heresy, although your holy sincerity would need the presence of many teachers, and not such a one as I am. In the first place, it is ignorantly and very dangerously (I will not say written, but) thought that it must not be accepted that a human being is the mother of God. You should know that this comes down from the impiety of the Nestorian heresy: Nestorius with profane daring did not fear to argue that blessed Mary was the mother only of a man, not also of God, and for this he was condemned by the severity of the catholic Church throughout the world. "It must not be accepted," it says, "that a human being is the mother of God." But where then is that saying, prophetic and evangelical alike: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel," which is interpreted, "God with us"? And again in the Gospel: "The holy one who will be born of you shall be called the Son of God"? Where too is that statement, received throughout all the islands and churches, which the authority of the fathers sets its seal on when it speaks against Nestorius: "Cursed," it says, "is whoever does not confess that the Son of God, true God, [?] was born of Mary for our salvation"?

Next you went on to say that God and man have one nature, and in this way that there is one substance of God. You would have spoken rightly if you had said this of the Trinity alone, where there is one and the same nature under the distinction of three persons. But when we come to the incarnation of the man who was assumed, just as we confess that there is one person of man and God, so we know that there is a twofold substance. Whoever asserts that the Lord our Redeemer is of one nature has denied either the man in the divinity or God in the body, since our redemption was accomplished not by one or the other but by both. But here, if you say [?] that there is one nature, that of God alone, then the divinity was crucified in the substance of its majesty; if you say there is one nature, of God alone, then the majesty died and was buried in its own substance. All these things God underwent not in himself but in the nature of the man he assumed. For God felt nothing with the feeling of one who suffers, yet he felt with the affection of one who suffers with another; he felt nothing by reason of the difference of substance, yet he felt by reason of the unity of the person. [?] … joined in unity, and then added: "We understand one and the same true man and true God"; and again: "We in no way doubt that he must be confessed true man and true God." Take this too from the hymn of the holy bishop and confessor Ambrose, which the catholic Church sings aloud on the Lord's Nativity through all the regions of Italy and Gaul: "Come forth from your bridal chamber, giant of twofold substance."

Amid all this, then, holy brother, flee the error of either side. If you speak only of the nature of God, you have imposed on God subjection to suffering and death; if you speak only of the nature of man, you have taken away from God the glory of redemption, taken away from the Creator the power of the Restorer. Hear how the sacred scriptures set forth both substances through one person. According to the divine nature he says, "I and the Father are one"; according to human substance he confesses, "The Father is greater than I"; according to the heavenly nature he declares, "All that the Father has is mine"; according to the weakness of earthly nature he says, "But the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." As man he declared, "My soul is sorrowful even to death"; as God he affirmed, "I have power to lay it down and power to take it up again." According to the nature of the flesh he hung on the cross; according to the substance of the divinity he was bestowing paradise and the heavenly kingdom.

The Arians, failing completely to see this because their hearts were darkened, since presumption and pride cloud the mind's vision, ascribed to God what belonged to the man, believing that the divinity was speaking as a lesser being where only the weakness of the man was being shown. Making no distinction between heavenly and earthly things, and refusing to accept two natures, of God and of man, they divided the substance of God; and by looking only at the words of the man, they lost from the light of their understanding God, who is the fullness of glory. And so whoever denies that the son of man is to be believed God is stained with the impiety of Nestorius, and whoever does not believe in two substances in the Redeemer is caught and entangled in the snare of Arius. But let us, my dearest brother, believe in Christ the Lord with so complete and inseparable a distinction that we know the person of God and man to be single and the substance twofold. As soul and body make one man, so divinity and humanity are one Christ.

You, however, forestalled by a twofold error, thought it right to write that, where two natures come together, it must not be accepted that God the Father is the father of a man, or that a human being is the mother of God. We, confidently and for our salvation, assert one person of God and man in him who was in the beginning and who, at the time of our redemption, was made in the likeness of sinful flesh, that is, in the reality of a man and in the likeness of a sinner. We, I say, bear witness that God the Father is the father of a man within the unity of the person, just as within the embrace of the same unity we confess a human being to be the mother of God, according to the authority of the Creed (to pass over other proofs), in which we say: "I believe also in the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary." If it is so great an error to have believed in a single and simple substance in the Lord our Saviour, how great an error is it to have asserted two persons? For if, in the union with the flesh he assumed, that form of a servant which God put on, there were not two substances, then God was not in the man, and the person of the man was separate from God. And so on such a view you will see a fourth person suddenly spring up from who knows where, and the understanding driven headlong by the logic of this perversity to the point where it would no longer be necessary to confess a Trinity.

Hear rather how blessed Isaiah sets out the birth of our Lord and Redeemer, in distinct order and with a distinction that yet holds together: "A child," he says, "is born to us, a son is given to us." Understand here the Son of God, born at the last stage of the ages from an unwed mother, nature knowing nothing of it and faith acting as husband; humbled by his own will; when the Holy Spirit came upon the virgin, man wondrously filled with God, and God mercifully changed into man; and that he did not empty out the greatness of his glory, but by taking on the condition of a servant showed the Lord's love. "A child is born to us, a son is given to us." He who already existed for himself was born for us. Given, then, from the divinity; born from the virgin. Born as one who would know death; given as one who knew no beginning. Born as one younger even than his mother; given as one than whom not even the Father was older. Born to die; given as the one through whom life would be born again. There he rules, here he is humbled; for himself he reigns, and for me he serves as a soldier. "A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and the government is upon his shoulder." The shoulder shows the man made visible; the government speaks of the hidden God. Recognise a twofold substance within the unity of a single person. From what is ours came what he paid out; from what is his own came what he bestowed. From ours he had the means to fall, from his own the means to rise again; from ours the means to be seized, from his own the means to show mercy; from ours he had the means to pay for us, from his own the means to appear in no way a debtor at all; from ours the means to be crucified, from his own the means to be glorified; from ours he gave the offering for sin, from his own he granted the grace of pardon. Thus his humiliation is shown to come from ours, his ascension from his own; from ours he offered the sacrifice, from his own he conferred the reward. Having in himself two natures, therefore, he is recognised as man by his weaknesses and proved to be God by his mighty works.

It wearies me to drag out my discourse in defending something so obvious. I know that I am rash to commit these very points, touched on briefly and summarily, either to my letters or to your understanding. But since you submit yourself with anxious humility to the healthy course of asking, you give me great hope of a remedy for this error. Draw back your foot, I beg you, from this danger, before you are swept by the torrent of pride into a depth from which there is no return; and keep your mind's judgement straight by disciplining it rather with the occupation of work, since it cannot bear the weight of much reading and does not know how to manage the treasure of knowledge. Moderate the immoderate rigour of your abstinence, which breeds weakness even in the mind, and which I think springs from the same source as your presumption in writing. Return to the royal road; flee that restless striving which nurses pride. And since we read, "It is not good to eat much honey" (for knowledge puffs up a poorly grounded mind more than it builds it up), beware of excessive reading, lest in a heart of little capacity you stir up a dangerous drunkenness, like that of wine taken too freely. Never trust your own thoughts; rather, read what you should imitate instead of writing what others should read, and say to the Lord in your mind: "In my heart I have hidden your words, that I may not sin against you." And if you wish to escape the dangers that are conceived within rather than those that assail from without, know that nothing is more useful for you than to fortify your life under some thoroughly proven abbot, to hand over your own will to the rules of an elder, and, so that you may overcome the snares of the adversary, to fear yourself.

I have thought it best to keep your little writing, or rather to suppress it, so that it may not pass any further into the hands and before the conscience of some other catholic who loves you less. From this you will be able to tell that the depths of your heart are sound: if you still listen attentively and willingly, as a free man, to me, your devoted friend, admonishing you humbly and lovingly. Before your question, your conviction might have seemed merely incautious; after this answer, your intention will appear inexcusable. But if in all this you think I am to blame for anything, since I wish your soul to be healed by bitter rather than sweet remedies, remember that the wounds of love are to be preferred to the kisses of flattery.
VIII. TO HIS MOST DEVOUT LORD AND SON RURICIUS, TO BE HONOURED BY ME IN CHRIST WITH SINGULAR AND HIGHEST ESTEEM, FROM FAUSTUS.

It is always a pleasure for me to talk with you in the very language of charity, with a heart undivided from yours, through any messenger at all, and to embrace you with all the eager attentiveness of courtesy. But now I have received the pledge of your affection all the more eagerly because it came so opportunely, through the service of a bearer from your household. When I met him, I found his merit greater than the report of him had told. I therefore rejoiced that he has grown up to be your gain: in him a better life has abolished the condition of his first birth, the freedom given by religion has wiped away the stain of his origin, and faith has emancipated one who was a slave and transferred him into adoption by Christ. In a ready and clear address you have set out the apostle's very broad provision for how we ought to deal with the milk-fed simplicity of this man and of the other brothers. And although that most learned page declares them to be less learned, we nevertheless admired in their purified conduct, through the gift of meekness and humility, the fullness of what they had read.

For the bounty of grace surpasses the instruction of learning. Even in a short time a candid purity of mind and an outstanding simplicity have entered their bright hearts and clear inner recesses, and through it the mirror of the divine image shines out in the brightness of the inner man. Of the divine image, I say, for this is what we read of the Lord: pure, simple, subtle. But that divine simplicity means something far different, since there is in us a twofold substance, of spirit and of flesh. What we have, we have received. The various gifts of the virtues have been added to us; they are not inborn. Without doubt, whatever can be taken away has been added. That we are good, we have borrowed from the goodness of our Maker. We live from him, but we are not life, as he is. We can be just; we cannot be justice. He is simple because nothing has been conferred on him by any added bounty. He who subsists of himself has taken nothing from elsewhere. God is alike living and life, good and goodness, merciful and mercy. In the glory of his virtues he himself is what he possesses. To put it in a word, man is gilded; God is gold. What in man is grace is in God nature. Therefore, since nothing has come to him from outside, nothing can be taken from him. He suffers no loss, because he knows no increase. He is the source both of himself and of the Son, because the spring and the river have one origin. Among those who are without beginning there is communion, not transfusion.

We read of the Son: He is the brightness of God's glory. As God was never without his brightness, so the Father was never without the majesty of the Son. The names of the two are of equal age, for unless the one were born, the other would not be called Father. In the same way the antiquity of the one fatherhood holds them together without separation. The Son is from the Father, yet not later than he, as the face is born of the head and yet is not found to be younger than its head. And so our God is neither confused in his proper persons nor divided. He is one power, divided neither in might nor in time. He is threefold in subsistence, because each person subsists in himself, and simple in substance, because, being one and unable to precede himself, he admits neither a later nor an earlier. From this simplicity we too have received a share, if there is nothing discordant in us, nothing changeable, nothing divided, and if by commendable efforts and by thoughts grounded in Christ we strive always to be the same, so that, being unchangeable in good, we may change only by fresh progress day by day.

Now to what a certain person asked from a desire to advance. It is a salutary and perfect plan to lighten the cares of the mind by dividing the management of one's earthly property among several people, and then to weigh three options carefully: whether it is better to lease out one's own portion, to administer it, or to sell it. The first would truly be good, namely that the servant of Christ should strive to walk, wholly poor, in the ways of the poor Christ, if he were free to seek out the perfect school of some great monastery, or at least the island warfare of an angelic community. For to practise the hermit's way of life in the middle of the world is as difficult as it is magnanimous.

The second shortcut for relieving the soul is to lay the burden of his property on those who act in his place. But he must look carefully into whether any of his sons can be equal to so demanding a service, lest perhaps the authority of the father's command against the father ..... [?] It is best, at this second level, to remain under an administrator [?], if either the will is present or the means have met the requirement of the annual payment.

The third option is to govern the portion of the property he keeps under his own lighter care, through the chosen help of faithful servants entrusted with the duties of stewardship, and to steer his course along the royal road with complete moderation.
