In advising this, I may seem to have in mind either our own advantage or that of the poor. In this arrangement there is no small gain if the ownership is sold while the use is kept. So, having briefly set out what comes first, what second and what third, we have left the choice to the judgment or the means of the one who asked. Let him for the fear and love of whom this question is being considered deign to show which is more fitting and which can more readily be carried out. May the Lord our God multiply his blessings upon you
with a long and happy life pleasing to him, most pious lord and son, whom I honour singularly in Christ with the highest honour.
9. To his lord and brother Ruricius, most closely bound to him and to be singularly honoured with all the virtue of devotion, Faustus.

By God's favour I have been placed in a retreat suited to religion and in the most tranquil silence, in which the Lord has applied the file of saving chastisement to the rust gathered through long security. In this repose, I say, I have been granted a great leisure, if we recognize it. While we win new citizens through the exchange of charity and rejoice in the salvation of those we have won, set amid these blessings we scorn our present exile and know that we have not lost our homeland but exchanged it. For while the faithful servants of God exercise the goodness of their devotion in our needs, we are owners without a home of our own and rich without possessions. Indeed, we enrich those who reap the fruit of consoling us. In a wonderful way our comforters do business with the poor and gain everlasting profit from the needy.

By the Lord's gift I have received this, the first of his bounties: that my most pious Ruricius, after the storms of this life, has turned the prow of salvation toward the harbour of religion, with the hand of the Most High at the helm; that after the shadows of seductive vanities and the illusions of passing dreams he has come to desire what is lasting and solid; and that, having at last despised the world, he has rejected its great unhappiness and gained happiness and profit for himself out of a perishing world. He has done so as faithfully as he hastens past collapsing things in flight, since by despising riches he has given away what could no longer give anything to his own use. So then, with as much eagerness as we once served in worldly pursuits, let us now serve the Lord with as much devotion. Your piety obliges me to speak rather severely with you for the curing of sins, and does not fear the reproach of that saying: The just man is his own accuser at the beginning. First of all, then, let us avoid slips of the mouth and of the heart. But as for the mouth, if you take care to set a guard on the heart, you will not have to labour to discipline the mouth. Whoever is careful in his thoughts will have no difficulty in setting a door of protection before his lips, for what the voice utters has first been shaped in the workshop of conscience. The outer man gives back what the inner man dictates. The mind gives the orders and the tongue serves, and that is why we are taught by the heavenly words: Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. What seems to be born from speech is first conceived in thought, so that the sound of the mouth will not bring forth what is unworthy if the mind prescribes what is just.

There are two kinds of fasting. The first is to restrain the appetite of incontinence from the wickedly alluring sweetness of pleasures, so that the outer and earthly man, tamed by the ploughshare of the cross, may waste away in a beneficial weakness. The other kind of abstinence is far loftier and far more precious, and no weakness can stand in its way. It is to govern the movements of the mind; to rein in, by the judgment of the inner man, irrational disturbances and the tumult of thoughts struggling among themselves; to join battle, with the authority of an angered faith, against hidden assaults and enemies within the household; and, through kindness, meekness, patience and tranquillity, to cultivate the image of God in the face of the inner man. The skill of the Maker stamped its beauty not on the outward person of the body but on the form of the soul.

Let sadness not break the man who meditates on spiritual and divine things, and let joy not undo him. Let the greatness of an even temper show a heart made firm in the fear of God, so that the notable opening of that book may also be applied to us. There the magnificent Elkanah, whose name means 'possession of God', is called in mystical language 'one man': There was, it says, one man. That is, he was always the same, because nothing in him appeared doubtful, double, changeable or divided. He remained in the state of the virtues, in unshaken order, so that adverse events did not move him and changing times did not change him, nor did light gusts of wind toss him this way and that, as they do the waves of the sea. So too let the watchful servant of God, grounded on the vast mass of faith, be changed only in this, by Christ working in him: that he is always clothed with new graces, and that useful things are planted in the field of his heart and harmful ones cut down. The divine word commanded its soldiers: When you go out to war and among the other spoils desire a virgin, you shall cut off her nails and her hair, and so join her to yourself in marriage. In the same way let us, girded with the fear of Christ, make the prudence of the world, which God made simple, uncorrupted and sincere, a captive subject to holy spiritual wisdom. Let us cut away its excesses, amputating its vices, and unite it to our heart in chaste union.

Above all, as far as we can with God's help, let us take care to conquer those passions of the five senses within us. Whatever is beautiful to the sight, whatever flatters the sense of smell, whatever entices the touch, whatever is sweet to the taste, whatever corrupts through the hearing: all these, if we abuse them, will turn the attention of the mind away from spiritual things toward earthly ones. Therefore, as the father of faith defeated those five kings with three hundred and eighteen men, by a mystery hidden within the letter, so let us strive, through the Lord's help and through his cross, to overcome these allurements of the five principal vices. For among the Greeks the sign of the cross and the sacred name of Jesus express the numbers of both reckonings. Those who overcome carnal pleasures with these weapons will deserve to hear: To him who conquers I will give the crown of life, and: He who conquers shall not be harmed by the second death.

That is why you easily despise earthly things, or give them out as a lender gives out money at interest. You think of that time when sinners will be burned up like hay; when those who neglected what was offered to them will burn in the everlasting fury of Gehenna, whose smoke goes up for ever and ever, and will be punished with such a death that they are not allowed to die in their pain, always dying to life and living to death without end. With a mind that looks ahead, I say, you set before your eyes that time of which we read: I will go into your house with burnt offerings. That is, laden with the fruit of good works and crowned with the insignia of justice, you will enter the door of life in triumph over the conquered flesh. Of that time we also read: The daughters of Tyre will worship him with gifts. That is, the souls won for Christ from the Gentiles will offer gifts to their Lord and will say with thanksgiving: Behold, I have multiplied the talent you gave me. Receive your loan back with interest, Lord. For then there will be a kind of trade in giving and receiving between man and God. Man will bring what he has laboured for, and God will repay what he promised. At that time you and your Sarah will be rewarded, each for the other, and adorned with a double crown for your salvation of one another, and you will deserve to hear: Well done, good and faithful servant; because you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord. Then you will marvel that the use of present things has passed into the ownership of eternal ones. And you will rejoice, glorified by those who disclosed your deeds, to have become their debtor by a happy exchange.

With dutiful affection we greet our inseparable son Leontius and your whole household, small and great alike. May the Lord our God multiply his blessings upon you with a long and happy life pleasing to him, lord and brother most closely bound to me and to be singularly honoured with all the virtue of devotion.
10. To his son Ruricius, lord most closely bound to him and to be especially honoured with distinguished honour, Faustus.

Thanks be to the Lord, who in his general provision has granted that the mind may travel freely between those whom distance separates, confined by no laws of absence, and that nothing should be so impenetrable that it does not lie open to the mind's gaze. Through the vision of the heart, with grace running between them, dear friends may see one another in the place where charity itself dwells. For our inner man also has his own eyes. With them, as witness of his conscience, he looks within; turned upon himself, he considers what he should blush for or rejoice in; he looks ahead to the last day. With them, thinking providently of the future, he sets before the face of his soul the history of his whole life, whether shameful or, by God's gift, praiseworthy. With anxious care he brings into the present the time when an account must be given, and with the brush of hope he paints on the secret page of his heart the things that God has prepared for those who love him.

These are the eyes, I think, that you too always lift up to the nod of the dreadful Judge, so that the prophetic saying may rightly be applied to you: The eyes of the wise man are in his head. That is why, for I have witnesses there who give you away, my son, that is why, I say, like an eager money-lender, you entrust the resources of present things, which must in any case be left behind, to the bosom of the Rewarder through the ransoms of captives, as a sower entrusts seed to the ground. You turn use into ownership and convert perishable things into everlasting treasures. That is why, with your most faithful Sarah, under the one yoke of Christ, you strive toward a common crown, despising earthly things and seeking heavenly ones, a pilgrim in the world and a candidate for paradise. As a secret soldier of Christ, you mock this world, which no longer has the means to deceive or seduce you. Together with the partner of your unending kingdom, by fasting and prayer and, as it were, with the hand of faith, you knock at the door of life in a holy conspiracy, so that you may win a double palm for your salvation of one another.

Yet amid all this, whatever is done is little: that incurable cases may be healed here, unquenchable fires quenched here, inescapable necessities overcome here; that the arrows of sin may be pulled out here from the vitals of the soul, wounds driven deep into the very marrow cured here, invisible stains atoned for here; that eternal joys may be bought here by the labour of faithful effort. That life will indeed be the reward of this one, but this one must be the price of that.

So, having first offered my respects, I ask that when a suitable opportunity arises you make us rejoice in news of your safety and prosperity [?]. I give abundant thanks for my sons and deacons. I greet with due reverence my lady daughter, a mirror of religion and an example of piety. May the Lord our God fill your goodness, which I must extol, with present blessings and make it worthy of eternal ones, lord most closely bound to me and to be especially honoured with distinguished honour, my son.
11. To his most blessed lord and brother, Bishop Ruricius, to be singularly honoured by him with the highest honour above all others, Faustus.

I have such confidence in the kindness of your heart that I am no longer content to draw from its purest fountain alone, but invite others as well to be refreshed with me by its waters. All the more so because its generosity, when extended, turns into gain for the giver, and the receiver is so rewarded by its goodness that the one who gives is not diminished but, like a loan at interest, grows by what he spends, most blessed lord, to be singularly honoured by me with the highest honour above all others.

So by this letter I pay you the debt of charity that can never be paid off, a payment that makes the payer richer, and I venture to offer you the material for a good work by commending those who are suffering. I trust that my recommendation is, so to speak, to your profit. And so I could not deny the bearer of this letter, who has endured captivity in the territory of Lyon, the mercy which the Church's humanity is accustomed to show to the wretched. Would that the generosity of the faithful could be as prompt as his need is all too plain! And since, though he himself has been released to some extent, he is held captive by the enslavement of his wife and children, I offer my respects and ask that you keep to the custom of your kindness in consoling him too, and support him with letters to those in authority wherever he asks.

My fellow servants, especially my brother the priest Memorius, your admirer, send their most reverent greetings with me. May the Lord our God preserve your holy beatitude, which remembers me, for a long and happy life for the advancement of his Church, most blessed lord and brother, to be singularly honoured by me with the highest honour above all others.
12. To his most blessed lord and brother, Bishop Ruricius, to be looked up to with due devotion and most worthy of his apostolic see, Faustus.

Thanks to you, as we write to you from our homeland: you made a homeland for us in our time abroad, and with untiring generosity you eased our longing for home. With one kindness following another, you brought a kind of pressure to bear on divine justice, so that what it had inflicted as chastisement it turned into honour, applied to consolation and changed into rest. It passed over our deserts in order to heap up yours, forgetting our debts and multiplying your gains. Exercising the greatness of its goodness toward both parties, it enriched us through your service and you through our exile. And so it came about that, impatient to wait, it already dispensed the blessing of the future in the present, and raised its most faithful servant onto the lampstand of its house, with mercy, justice, sincerity, continence and kindness, his own household supporters, working together. See at what price my Ruricius purchased the highest priesthood! What he bought with is the very thing he bought, and with his own witnesses acclaiming him he displayed in himself both the grounds for honour and the shrinking from it [?]. He who knew how to acquire so great a gift therefore knows how to guard it in Christ's name.

I commend to you the bearer of this letter, the holy priest Florentius, long known to me and adorned both with the examples of his master and with the flowers of good conduct. He is travelling to obtain the release of his sister, and he has welcomely offered himself to me as a timely go-between. We greet your whole household, elders and young alike, with fatherly affection. My fellow servants, your debtors and admirers, send their most reverent greetings with me. May our Lord preserve your beatitude, which I must extol, for a long and complete life, for the advancement of his Church and for our joy, most blessed lord and brother, to be looked up to with due devotion and most worthy of your apostolic see.

In the treatise appended to the letter that Pope John II sent to Caesarius in the year 534, concerning the case of a certain bishop who had been deposed from the episcopate because of the disgrace of a crime he had committed, the following is read (cf. Concilia antiqua Galliae, ed. Sirmond, I 235):

'And this must be carefully noted. According to what is written above, those clerics who return to their own wives are completely suspended from office. Even men who have married twice, or the husbands of women previously married, who are certainly doing something lawful, still cannot be ordained clerics, or if they have been ordained, are deposed. Of these the holy bishop Faustus also says in his letter: He loses the grace of consecration who still wishes to perform the office of a husband.'

Whether these words come from a letter or rather from one of Faustus's sermons is, to my mind, uncertain. That sermons are sometimes called letters is shown, among other evidence, by the heading of Faustus's first sermon preserved in the Durlach codex 36 (cf. p. 223, note on line 3).
